de.form.simulation.hint: The seed, the number of futures and the number format belong to this browser, not to a plan: switching plans keeps the same futures.

de.form.spending.hint: {month} a month, today's money, taxes after stopping included
de.form.spending.spenddown: Not used by the spend-down, which works out its own. Still the unit of “years of spending” and of the cash cushion.

de.form.stockVol.hint: World stocks: about 15–18%. For a calmer portfolio, lower the stock share under Portfolio mix instead.
de.form.tails.hint: Fat tails make −40% years about 8× more frequent, with calmer ordinary years.
de.form.tentShare: Stock share at the FIRE start
de.form.tentShare.none: Same as normal: no bond tent.
de.grid.floor.axis: Floor: the least you'd spend ({currency}, today's)
de.grid.floor.desc: The spend-down works out its own spending, so the columns are its floor: how often the floor could always be paid, for each FIRE start. Same random markets throughout. Tap a cell to try that plan.
de.grid.floor.title: When can you stop, with which floor?
de.grid.spending.desc: How often the money lasts for each FIRE start and spending level, on the same random markets throughout. Around 90% is a common target for a plan you can't easily undo. Tap a cell to try that plan.
de.grid.spending.title: When can you stop, at which spending?
de.guide.title: Guide
de.help._stress.html: Replaces the first years after the FIRE start with a historical-style crash in every future; the years after it stay random. Shows how the plan copes with the worst moment for a crash.
de.help._stress.title: Force a crash at the FIRE start
de.help._tails.html:
With a normal distribution, a −40% year almost never happens. “Fat tails” make extreme years several times more frequent (and ordinary years a bit calmer), capped at −60% and +60% real in a year.

Over a long plan they change the result very little, usually by less than a point: the years swing as much as before on average, and a few extreme years even out over decades. What breaks a plan is a crash right after you stop, and the stress test shows that.

30,000 a year from 1,000,000, from age 50 to 95: the money lasts in about 76% of futures, with fat tails (t, 6) too; with a −40% first year, in about 36%.

The number in “(t, 6)” sets how fat: it's a Student-t distribution with that many degrees of freedom. The lower it is, the fatter the tails.
de.help._tails.title: Extreme years
de.help.account.contrib.html: What goes into the account each year until the FIRE start (yours and your employer's), in today's money.
de.help.account.contrib.title: Paid in per year
de.help.account.growth.html: Like the portfolio: invested in the same stock/bond mix, with the same random returns. At a fixed interest: credited a steady rate every year (a pension fund that guarantees an interest, a savings account).
de.help.account.growth.title: Grows
de.help.account.tax.html:
The tax on taking the money out, as one blended rate on the whole balance.

15% of 200,000 = 30,000 tax, 170,000 into the portfolio.
de.help.account.tax.title: Tax when withdrawn
de.help.account.unlock_age.html:
The owner's age when the account is taken out and added to the portfolio. Until then a future in which the reachable money runs out fails, even if this account would have saved it.

Typical: 59½ in the US, 57 in the UK (from 2028), 60 for Swiss 3a and 58–65 for pillar 2. Check your own rules.
de.help.account.unlock_age.title: Unlocks at age
de.help.accounts.html:
Money you can't reach until an age: a 401(k) or IRA, a workplace pension taken as a lump sum, a personal pension, a pillar 2 or 3a. Until its owner reaches the unlock age it counts in your wealth but can't pay the bills; then it is withdrawn, taxed, and added to the portfolio.

Pensions paid as a monthly amount for life go under “Income and costs after stopping”.
de.help.accounts.title: Retirement accounts
de.help.backup.html:
Saved plans live in this browser's storage, on this device only. Browsers can clear it:

  • clearing the browsing data or the site's data;
  • a private window, when it closes;
  • Safari (on a Mac, iPhone or iPad) deletes a site's data once you've used it for 7 days without visiting the site, unless you added the site to the Home Screen;
  • some browsers free space when the device runs low.

When you first save, the page asks the browser to keep its storage for good (Firefox asks you; Chrome and Edge decide on their own). That protects against the last case, not the others.

Export plans writes every plan to a file: the only backup that survives a cleared browser or a lost device. A note under the plan reminds you when saved changes aren't in an exported file yet. To restore, use Import plans.
de.help.backup.title: Backups
de.help.bond_return.html: The compound yearly growth of the bond part, before inflation. What counts is the return after inflation: high-quality bonds have often earned about 0–2% real.
de.help.bond_return.title: Bond return (nominal)
de.help.bond_vol.html:
How much bond returns swing from year to year. Broad high-quality bond funds: roughly 4–7%.

The simulator keeps inflation the same every year, so bonds swing less here than in years when inflation jumps: in 2022, broad US bond funds lost about 13% before inflation. With bonds in your mix, try a higher bond volatility for a cautious case.
de.help.bond_vol.title: Bond volatility
de.help.cash.html: Today's bank balances. They grow at the cash interest minus inflation, so in today's money they usually shrink. Spending is paid from cash first.
de.help.cash.title: Cash today
de.help.cash_buffer_years.html: At the FIRE start, this many years of spending are moved from the portfolio to cash, and spent first, whatever the markets do. The idea: not having to sell in an early crash. In this model it usually helps little, because cash loses value to inflation and misses the recovery.
de.help.cash_buffer_years.title: Cash cushion
de.help.cash_interest.html:
What your bank accounts pay, before inflation.

1% with 2% inflation → cash loses about 1% a year in today's money.
de.help.cash_interest.title: Cash interest
de.help.chart.dist.html: Left: how wealth at the FIRE start is spread across futures. Right: in which years the failing futures run out. Bars before the last account unlocks mean the bridge was too thin.
de.help.chart.dist.title: Distributions
de.help.chart.grid.html:
Each cell: how often the money lasts if you stop in that year (row) and spend that much (column). The outlined cell is your plan. Tap a cell to try that plan.

With guardrails or Vanguard, a floor and ceiling you set yourself keep the columns between them. Left as they came, around the spending, they move with it: each column has its own, as when you change the spending.

With the spend-down, which works out its own spending, the columns are its floor, up to its ceiling.
de.help.chart.grid.title: When can you stop, at which spending?
de.help.chart.paths.html:
Each thin line is one future: purple = poorest, yellow = richest, red = runs out. Black line: median; dashed: 10th percentile; shaded: middle 50% and 80% of futures. Dotted lines mark the FIRE start, accounts unlocking, income starting and one-off events.

Years of spending = wealth ÷ yearly spending: 25 means 25 years of spending in the bank.
de.help.chart.paths.title: Wealth over time
de.help.chart.safe.html:
The highest yearly spending that lasts in 90% (solid) and 95% (dotted) of futures, for each FIRE start. Hover or tap for the withdrawal rate it implies.

With the spend-down it shows what the spend-down allows in the first year if you stop in each year instead: in the median future, and in the worst and best 10%, depending on how the years until then went.
de.help.chart.safe.title: Safe spending by FIRE start
de.help.chart.spending.html: For flexible rules: each line is one future's yearly spending. The shaded area holds 80% of the futures that last. Dashed: your starting spending (not for the spend-down, where each future starts at its own); dotted: floor and ceiling.
de.help.chart.spending.title: What you'd get to spend
de.help.chart.stress.html: Your plan with a crash forced into the first years after the FIRE start, for every rule. Shows which rule holds up best when things go wrong at the worst moment.
de.help.chart.stress.title: Stress test
de.help.concept.about.html:
No ads, no accounts, no tracking. The code is public, on GitHub, under the MIT license.

  • Something broken, or a number that looks wrong? Open an issue, with made-up numbers: issues are public.
  • No GitHub account, or rather not post in public? Write to hello@whencanistop.fyi.
  • If it's useful to you, you can support it: ☕ Buy me a coffee
de.help.concept.about.title: Free and open source
de.help.concept.monte-carlo.html:
The simulator plays your plan through thousands of possible market histories, each year getting a random return. “Money lasts in 85%” means: in 85 of 100 of those futures, the money paid every year's spending until the end of the plan.

It's not a forecast of one future, but a measure of how robust the plan is across many.
de.help.concept.monte-carlo.title: What a simulated future is
de.help.concept.privacy.html:
Everything runs in your browser: the simulation, the charts, the saving. Nothing you type is sent anywhere, there are no accounts and no tracking.

  • Plans are kept in this browser (its local storage). Clearing the site's data, a private window, or Safari's clean-up of sites you haven't visited lately loses them: use Export plans to keep a copy.
  • To move plans to another device, export them there and import the file.
  • A share link carries one plan inside the link itself, after the “#”: browsers never send that part to the site. Whoever gets the link can see the numbers.
  • You don't have to take this on trust: the code is public, so anyone can check that nothing is sent, on GitHub.

The privacy notice says who runs this site, what its host receives, and how to reach them.
de.help.concept.privacy.title: Your numbers stay with you
de.help.concept.sequence.html: A crash right after you stop working does far more damage than the same crash 20 years later: you sell at low prices to pay the bills, and that money never recovers. This is called sequence-of-returns risk. The stress test shows it.
de.help.concept.sequence.title: Why the first years matter most
de.help.concept.swr.html:
The share of your wealth you can take out in the first year, then keep spending the same real amount, and still not run out. The famous “4% rule” comes from 30-year US retirements; for 40+ years, or for markets around the world, studies of the past find around 3–3.5%.

The simulator finds less with its default returns: about 3% over 30 years and 2–2.5% over 45, in 90% of futures. Its returns are below the past century's, and each year is drawn on its own, so nothing pulls a bad decade back towards the average. “Safe spending by FIRE start” shows the rate for your plan.

1,200,000 × 3% = 36,000 a year.
de.help.concept.swr.title: Safe withdrawal rate (SWR)
de.help.concept.todays-money.html:
All amounts mean today's purchasing power, in every year. The simulator takes inflation out of the returns instead of adding it to the prices.

40,000 a year in 2050 buys what 40,000 buys today, even though the bills in 2050 will show bigger numbers.

So enter spending, savings and pensions at today's prices. Returns and interest rates are entered as usual (nominal); the simulator subtracts the inflation you set.
de.help.concept.todays-money.title: Everything is in today's money
de.help.contrib.html: What you add to the investments each year until you stop, in today's money (so in real life it rises with inflation). Contributions to retirement accounts are set on each account.
de.help.contrib.title: Saved per year until the FIRE start
de.help.contrib_growth.html:
How much more you save each year, above inflation: raises and promotions. Applies to the retirement accounts' contributions too.

2% → 20,000 this year, 20,400 next year, about 26,900 in 15 years.
de.help.contrib_growth.title: Saving rises by
de.help.currency.html: The currency of all the plan's amounts. It only changes how numbers are shown: there's no conversion, and the market assumptions are yours to set for it.
de.help.currency.title: Currency
de.help.end_person.html:
How long the plan has to work: until this person reaches this age. Pick the youngest person, and an age you'd be unlucky to outlive: longer horizons need a lower withdrawal rate.

For a couple, the chance that at least one of you lives into their 90s is much higher than either one's alone: plan for the longest-lived of you.
de.help.end_person.title: Money must last until
de.help.events.html:
A single amount in a single year, before or after the FIRE start: an inheritance or the sale of a house (positive), a new roof, a car, a wedding, help for a child (negative). In today's money, after any tax. A cost the money can't pay is a failure in its year.

To leave money to someone, enter it as a cost in the year the plan ends: a future that ends with less than that fails.
de.help.events.title: One-off events
de.help.files.html: Export plans downloads all saved plans as one file: your backup, and the way to move them to another browser or device. Import plans adds the plans in such a file to the ones here (nothing is replaced).
de.help.files.title: Export and import
de.help.fire_year.html:
The first year you live from your savings: FIRE stands for financial independence, retire early. Until then you keep earning and saving; from then on, savings stop and spending starts.

Each year later adds a year of savings and growth, and is one year less to fund. The grid below shows the neighbouring years side by side.
de.help.fire_year.title: FIRE start
de.help.income.html:
Money that comes in, or goes out on top of the spending, for a stretch of the retirement: a state pension, a company pension paid monthly, part-time work, rent from a flat; or a mortgage until it's paid off, children at university. In Switzerland, someone who stops working before 65 still pays AHV contributions, set by their wealth: a cost until 65.

  • A positive amount is income, a negative one an extra cost. Per year, in today's money.
  • It counts from the FIRE start at the earliest: before that, your savings already reflect what you earn.
  • It reduces (or adds to) what the portfolio has to pay each year.
de.help.income.indexed.html:
How the line's amount moves over the years:

  • Rises with inflation: it keeps its value in today's money, like most state pensions.
  • Faster or slower than inflation: it rises by the % you set compared with inflation, from the year after its first. A negative % falls behind inflation.
  • Fixed in money: the same amount of money every year, so inflation shrinks its value, like a pension that is never raised or a fixed-rate mortgage. Enter the amount as it will be paid.

A pension that falls behind inflation, −1% a year: 20,000 is worth about 18,100 in today's money after 10 years.

Health insurance that gets dearer faster than inflation: a cost line of −6,000, +2% a year → about 7,300 a year after 10 years. Then leave it out of the spending per year, or it counts twice.

A line that started before this year changes from this year on.
de.help.income.indexed.title: Each year
de.help.income.title: Income and costs after stopping
de.help.income.when.html:
When a line starts and when it stops, in one of three ways:

  • In the year: a calendar year.
  • When someone turns: an age, so it follows their birth year.
  • FIRE start + years: moves with the FIRE start, so every FIRE start on the grid keeps “part-time for the first 5 years” right.

A line stops in its stop year: stopping at “FIRE start + 5” pays for 5 years.
de.help.income.when.title: Starts and stops
de.help.inflation.html: Turns the nominal inputs (returns, interest) into today's money. It doesn't raise your spending: that's already in today's money.
de.help.inflation.title: Inflation
de.help.locale.html: How numbers are written and read: which mark separates thousands and which one decimals. Your browser's language by default. It's a setting of this browser, not of a plan.
de.help.locale.title: Number format
de.help.n_sims.html:
How many futures to simulate. More = more precise, but slower.

10,000 → “money lasts” is within about ±1 point, 19 times in 20; 50,000 → about ±0.4.
de.help.n_sims.title: Simulated futures
de.help.people.html:
Everyone whose age matters to the plan: whose retirement accounts unlock at an age, whose pension starts at an age, and who the money has to last for. Up to four.

Only the birth year is used: the simulation moves a year at a time.
de.help.people.title: People
de.help.plans.html:
A plan is your situation and the choices you're trying, saved under a name in this browser. Keep several to compare: “Stop at 50”, “Stop at 55, part-time”, “Spend less”.

  • Pick one in the list to load it.
  • Change any value: the plan shows as edited, and a dot marks each changed field. Save (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S) keeps the changes; Revert brings back the saved values. Unsaved changes survive a reload.
  • Under ⋯: a new plan from scratch, a copy of this one, rename, delete, share, export and import.
  • Deleting, reverting, or switching away from unsaved changes shows an Undo for a few seconds.

The random seed and the number of futures aren't part of a plan: switching keeps the same futures, so the comparison is fair.
de.help.plans.title: Plans
de.help.portfolio.html:
Today's value of the investments you can sell at any time: brokerage accounts, funds, shares. They grow at the random return of the stock/bond mix under “Portfolio mix”.

Retirement accounts you can't touch until an age go under “Retirement accounts” instead.
de.help.portfolio.title: Invested today
de.help.portfolio_tax.html:
An effective tax rate on what you take out of the portfolio (not cash), for countries that tax capital gains or dividends when you sell. Each withdrawal is grossed up: to spend 100 you sell 100 ÷ (1 − rate).

A 25% tax on gains when about half of what you sell is gain → about 12%.

If your taxes in retirement are already in the spending, leave it at 0.
de.help.portfolio_tax.title: Tax on portfolio withdrawals
de.help.result.compare.html: Your plan with each spending rule, on the same markets. Tap one to switch. “n/a”: your spending is outside that rule's floor–ceiling range.
de.help.result.compare.title: Same plan, other rules
de.help.result.end.html: The wealth left when the plan ends, in today's money, across all futures (failed ones count as 0). The typical future often ends rich: over many decades an average market compounds a lot. It's the same plan that runs out in the bad futures, which is why flexible rules let you spend more in the good ones.
de.help.result.end.title: Wealth at the end
de.help.result.fail.html: The share of futures in which the money runs out, and in those futures only the typical (median) year it happens. The last part: how many run out before the last retirement account unlocks (the “bridge” the reachable money has to carry alone).
de.help.result.fail.title: Runs out
de.help.result.first.html: Only for the spend-down: what it works out for the year of the FIRE start, before the floor and ceiling. It depends on how the markets go until you stop. With the FIRE start in the year of the balances it is one number, the same in every future.
de.help.result.first.title: First-year spending (spend-down)
de.help.result.flex.html: Only for flexible rules, among the futures that last: the typical spending over the whole retirement, the lowest yearly spending (in the worst 10% of futures), and how many futures spend at least one year at the floor.
de.help.result.flex.title: Average spending, leanest year, reaching the floor
de.help.result.rate.html: First year's spending ÷ the median wealth at the start. Comparable with an SWR, but the income lines and the retirement accounts unlocking later also help.
de.help.result.rate.title: Starting withdrawal rate
de.help.result.start.html: What you'd have when you stop: investments, cash, and the retirement accounts (net of their withdrawal tax). Uncertain too, because the years until then have random markets.
de.help.result.start.title: Wealth at the FIRE start
de.help.result.success.html:
The share of simulated futures in which every year's spending could be paid until the end. Green from 90%, amber from 75%. About 90% is a common target for a plan you can't easily undo.

Careful when comparing rules: with fixed spending it means the full amount was always paid; with a flexible rule only that spending never had to go below the floor.
de.help.result.success.title: Money lasts in …
de.help.rule.adjust.html:
How much spending changes when a guardrail is crossed.

10% → 42,000 becomes 37,800 after a cut, 46,200 after a raise.
de.help.rule.adjust.title: Cut / raise by
de.help.rule.assumed_return.html: The real yearly return the spend-down works out its amount with. If the money earns exactly this, spending stays the same every year; if more, it rises; if less, it falls. Below the stocks' median it is a safety margin: about 2 points below is a sensible start.
de.help.rule.assumed_return.title: Assumed return (spend-down)
de.help.rule.band.html:
How far the withdrawal rate may drift from where it started before spending changes. Smaller = more frequent adjustments.

20% → with a 3.5% start, nothing happens between 2.8% and 4.2%.
de.help.rule.band.title: Guardrail band
de.help.rule.ceiling.html:
The most you'd want to spend in good times. Without it, a flexible rule could keep raising spending in very good futures.

Guardrails and Vanguard start at your spending, so it has to sit between the floor and the ceiling. Until you set them yourself they sit around the spending (−20%, +25%) and move with it. Once you set them, they stay, and the spending slider keeps within them.
de.help.rule.ceiling.title: Ceiling
de.help.rule.down.html: The most spending may fall in one year, however bad the markets were. Vanguard uses 2.5% in nominal terms.
de.help.rule.down.title: Max cut per year
de.help.rule.fixed.html: The same real amount every year, whatever the markets do. Simple and predictable, but it must survive the worst decades unchanged, so it's the strictest test: the classic “safe withdrawal rate”.
de.help.rule.fixed.title: Fixed spending
de.help.rule.floor.html:
The lowest spending you'd accept: the costs you can't cut (housing, health, food, taxes). A flexible rule never goes below it, and a future fails only when even the floor can't be paid.

32,000 under a 40,000 plan: the essentials, with travel and extras cut.
de.help.rule.floor.title: Floor
de.help.rule.guardrails.html:
Your withdrawal rate (what the portfolio pays ÷ wealth) at the start is the reference. Each year:

  • rate more than the band above the start (wealth fell) → spending is cut by the percentage in Cut / raise by;
  • rate more than the band below the start (wealth grew) → spending is raised by it;
  • otherwise unchanged. Always between floor and ceiling.

1,200,000 and 42,000 → rate 3.5%. With a 20% band and a 10% cut / raise: below about 1,000,000 (rate 4.2%) spending is cut to 37,800; above 1,500,000 (rate 2.8%) it rises to 46,200. Cuts can repeat in a long bad stretch.
de.help.rule.guardrails.title: Guardrails (Guyton & Klinger)
de.help.rule.max_cut.html: The most spending may fall in one year. A smaller limit means gentler cuts, but they come later, so the money runs out more often. With no limit (100%) and no floor it can never run out: spending takes all the bad luck.
de.help.rule.max_cut.title: Max cut per year (spend-down)
de.help.rule.max_raise.html: The most spending may rise in one year. What isn't spent yet stays for the following years.
de.help.rule.max_raise.title: Max raise per year (spend-down)
de.help.rule.spenddown.html:
Each year it works out what you could spend every year until the end, the same each year, if the money earned the assumed return, and aims at that. Counted as money today: what you can reach, the retirement accounts still locked (after their tax), and all future income and costs. Until an account unlocks only the reachable money pays the bills, so the amount is never more than that money alone can carry until then.

Every year the amount is worked out again from the actual balances. Spending doesn't jump to it: it moves towards it by at most +raise / −cut a year, always between floor and ceiling. The spending per year above isn't used.

It doesn't plan to keep money, so it spends more and leaves less. A crash right after you stop hurts it more, because it spends more in the first years.

Once you've stopped, it gives the year's amount: enter that January's balances, set the FIRE start to that year, and read “First-year spending”.
de.help.rule.spenddown.title: Spend-down (die with zero)
de.help.rule.up.html: The most spending may rise in one year, however good the markets were. Vanguard uses 5% in nominal terms, about 3% in today's money.
de.help.rule.up.title: Max raise per year
de.help.rule.vanguard.html:
Each year the target is your starting withdrawal rate × current wealth (plus income). Spending moves towards it, but by at most the max raise or the max cut a year. Always between floor and ceiling.

Markets −30% → the target drops 30%, but spending only falls 2.5% a year while it stays down. Smoother than guardrails, slower to react to a deep crash.
de.help.rule.vanguard.title: Vanguard dynamic spending
de.help.seed.html: Picks the set of random futures. The same seed always gives the same futures, so when you change the plan you compare it on the same markets. New seed draws a different set: if the result moves more than about a point, use more futures.
de.help.seed.title: Random seed
de.help.share.html:
A link that opens a copy of this plan in someone else's browser (or yours, on another device). The plan is packed into the link itself, after the “#”, which browsers never send to the site: nothing is uploaded. The person opening it gets their own copy; changes on either side don't reach the other. Opening the same link again goes to that copy instead of adding another.

The link also says which seed and how many futures you used. If theirs are different, a note under their plan says so, since the numbers can then differ a little, and offers to use the same.

Anyone with the link sees every number in the plan, unless you give it a password: the plan and its name are then encrypted in your browser, and the link opens only with that password. The password isn't in the link, so send it another way, not in the same message.

Whoever holds a locked link can try passwords on their own computer, as many as they like, so pick a long one: a few unrelated words beat a short word with symbols. A forgotten password can't be recovered: share the plan again with a new one.

de.help.spending.html:
What the household will spend each year after stopping, in today's money, including the taxes of those years (income tax on withdrawals, health insurance you'll now pay yourself, unless you give it a line of its own below). Leave out costs that stop with work, such as commuting.

40,000 a year = 3,333 a month. With a flexible rule this is the starting amount. The spend-down works out its own and doesn't use it.

Costs that come and go (a mortgage until it's paid off, children's school) are better as lines under “Income and costs after stopping”, and so are costs that rise faster than inflation, such as health insurance. A cost entered as a line is left out of the spending, or it counts twice.

A tax on wealth (a wealth tax, a yearly stamp duty on investments) shrinks as the portfolio does: take its rate off the stock and bond returns instead.

A 0.3% wealth tax: stocks 6% → 5.7%, bonds 3% → 2.7%.
de.help.spending.title: Spending per year
de.help.start_year.html: The year and month your balances are from. The simulation starts there, and only the rest of that year still grows and saves. Update it whenever you update the balances.
de.help.start_year.title: Balances as of
de.help.stock_bond_corr.html: Whether stocks and bonds tend to move together: −1 opposite, 0 independent, +1 together. Negative helps a mix (bonds rise when stocks crash). It was negative most of 2000–2020 and positive in inflation years such as 2022.
de.help.stock_bond_corr.title: Stock/bond correlation
de.help.stock_return.html:
The typical yearly growth of stocks, before inflation. It is the compound growth rate: half the simulated years are better, half worse, and over the long run wealth grows at this rate (the simple average of the years is higher). The simulator subtracts inflation.

6% with 2% inflation ≈ 3.9% real: around the middle of long-run forecasts for world stocks (about 3.5–5% real). World stocks have earned about 5% real a year since 1900.

A return from elsewhere may be the simple average of the years instead: for the same stocks it's higher by about half the volatility squared.

An average of 7.4% with 17% volatility ≈ 6% here.

This one input moves the result more than any other: try a cautious case.
de.help.stock_return.title: Stock return (nominal median)
de.help.stock_share.html: How much of the portfolio (and of the retirement accounts invested like it) is in stocks; the rest is in bonds. Every year it is brought back to this share (rebalanced). Less in stocks = smaller swings, but slower growth, before and after you stop.
de.help.stock_share.title: Stock share
de.help.stock_vol.html:
How much stock returns swing from year to year (their standard deviation). Higher volatility hurts a withdrawal plan, even with the same median.

17% (world stocks) → 2 years in 3 between about −11% and +22% real.

Don't lower it to model a calmer portfolio: lower volatility only comes with a lower return. Lower the stock share instead, which changes both together.
de.help.stock_vol.title: Stock volatility
de.help.stress-custom.html:
Real returns in %, one per year from the FIRE start, separated by commas. Where the decimal mark is a comma, put a space after the commas between years: -12,5, -20.

-30, 10, -15 → −30% in the first year, +10% in the second, −15% in the third.
de.help.stress-custom.title: Custom crash
de.help.tent_share.html:
A lower stock share only around the FIRE start, the moment a crash hurts most. Before and after, you're back at the normal stock share.

Normally 100%, 70% at the start, 4 years to get there, 8 back: 92.5%, 85%, 77.5% in the years before, 70% in the year of the FIRE start, then up 3.75 points a year.

Set it equal to the stock share for no tent.
de.help.tent_share.title: Bond tent
de.help.tent_years.html: How gradually the stock share moves down to the tent before the FIRE start, and back up afterwards, in equal steps. 0 years before = the switch happens at the start.
de.help.tent_years.title: Years to get there, years back

de.page.hero.label: Money lasts in
de.page.how.advice: This is a tool for thinking about a plan, not financial advice.
de.page.how.limits.inflation: Inflation is the rate you set, in every year: only the returns are random.
de.page.how.limits.markets: Real markets have long bad stretches and recoveries; independent random years are a simplification. Use the stress test for bad starts.
de.page.how.limits.missing: Not modelled: pension reforms, how long each person lives (the plan simply runs until the age you set), currency risk.
de.page.how.limits.returns: The return assumption moves the answer more than anything else. Try a cautious case.
de.page.how.limits.taxes: Taxes are simplified: a flat rate on each retirement account when it unlocks, and optionally an effective rate on portfolio withdrawals. Put income tax and health insurance into the spending, and take a tax on wealth off the returns.
de.page.how.money.text: Returns are drawn after inflation, so a spending of 40,000 a year means today's purchasing power in every year. Nominal inputs (returns, interest rates) are converted using the inflation you set.
de.page.how.rules.band: The flexible rules stay between the floor (costs you can't cut) and the ceiling. They fail only when even the floor can't be paid.
de.page.how.rules.fixed: Fixed: the same real amount every year (the classic safe withdrawal rate).
de.page.how.rules.guardrails: Guardrails (Guyton & Klinger): cut spending when the withdrawal rate drifts above where it started by more than the band, raise it when it drifts below.
de.page.how.rules.spenddown: Spend-down (die with zero): each year, aim at what could be spent every year until the end if the money earned the assumed return, with the locked accounts and future income counted as money today; until an account unlocks, only the reachable money pays. Spending moves towards it by at most +raise / −cut a year.
de.page.how.rules.vanguard: Vanguard dynamic: aim at a fixed share of wealth, but change spending by at most +raise / −cut a year.
de.page.how.summary: How the simulation works, and what it can't see
de.page.how.years.cash: Cash and fixed-interest accounts grow at their interest minus inflation. Until the FIRE start you keep saving.
de.page.how.years.fail: Spending comes from cash first, then the portfolio. A future fails in the first year the reachable money can't pay the bills, even if a retirement account would unlock later.
de.page.how.years.income: From the FIRE start, income lines (pensions, part-time work) and extra costs count, each rising with inflation, faster or slower than it, or fixed in money; one-off events happen in their year.
de.page.how.years.portfolio: The portfolio, and the retirement accounts invested like it, is a mix of stocks and bonds rebalanced every year. Stocks and bonds each get one random return per year, drawn independently from a log-normal distribution with the median and spread you set (or a fat-tailed one).
de.page.how.years.unlock: When its owner reaches the unlock age, a retirement account is withdrawn, taxed, and added to the portfolio.

de.privacy.advice.text: When can I stop? is a tool for thinking about a plan. It is not financial advice and not a forecast. It is free, and provided as it is, without any warranty (MIT license). What you decide about your money is up to you.
de.privacy.backLink: Back to When can I stop?
de.privacy.changes.text: A new version of this notice is published here, with its date. Every earlier version is in the project's history on GitHub.
de.privacy.description: What When can I stop? keeps on your device, what its host receives, who runs it, and how to reach them. No account, no cookies, no analytics, no tracking.
de.privacy.device.exported: when you last exported your plans, for the reminder to keep a backup.
de.privacy.device.offline: Once the site has loaded, a service worker also keeps a copy of the site's own files, so that it works offline. It holds nothing about you. The site sets no cookies.
de.privacy.device.settings: your settings: the random seed, the number of simulated futures, the number format, the language and the theme you picked, which sections of the form are open, and whether you closed the welcome note;
de.privacy.device.storage: your saved plans, and the plan on screen with its unsaved changes;
de.privacy.device.text: The simulation runs in your browser. The page keeps these in the browser's local storage, on your device only, and never sends them anywhere:
de.privacy.device.why: They're there for what you ask the page to do: keep your plans, and carry on where you left off. They stay until you delete them, in the page or by clearing this site's data in your browser's settings.
de.privacy.files.text: Export plans saves a file on your device. A share link carries one plan inside the link itself, after the “#”, which browsers never send to a server: the link goes only where you send it. Anyone who has it can open the plan, unless you lock it with a password.
de.privacy.host.basis: For visitors protected by the GDPR, the legal basis is the operator's legitimate interest in a secure, working website (Article 6(1)(f) GDPR).
de.privacy.host.cloudflare: Cloudflare uses this to deliver the site and to protect it from attacks, and keeps it in its logs, as its privacy policy describes.
de.privacy.host.logs: This site also has Cloudflare's Workers Logs turned on, to find problems. Whatever they record about a request is kept for 3 days, can be read only in the site's Cloudflare account, and isn't used for anything else.
de.privacy.host.text: The site is hosted by Cloudflare (Cloudflare, Inc., USA). Like any web host, Cloudflare receives what your browser sends to fetch each file: your IP address, which file was asked for, when, and browser details (the user agent). Besides opening the page, your browser asks for the site's files again while it's open, from time to time, to check for a new version.
de.privacy.host.transfers: Cloudflare does this on the operator's behalf, under its data processing addendum. It has data centres around the world and is based in the USA. Transfers rely on Cloudflare's certification under the EU-U.S. and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, and on the EU standard contractual clauses in its data processing addendum, which also cover data protected by Swiss law.
de.privacy.links.text: The page links to GitHub, for the code, and to Buy Me a Coffee. Nothing is loaded from them unless you click a link; once you're there, their own privacy policies apply.
de.privacy.rights.complain: You can also complain to a data protection authority: in Switzerland, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC); in the EU or the EEA, the authority where you live.
de.privacy.rights.text: You can ask what data about you the operator has, have it corrected or deleted, or object to its use: write to privacy@whencanistop.fyi. In practice the operator has nothing about you beyond those few days of request logs.
de.privacy.summary: In short: what you type into When can I stop? stays on your device. There is no account, no cookie, no analytics and no tracking, and the page loads nothing from other sites. The only data that reaches anyone is what every browser sends to fetch a web page, and it never contains your plans.
de.privacy.title: Privacy · When can I stop?
de.privacy.who.text: whencanistop.fyi is run by Gabriele Ardizzone, in Switzerland, as a free, non-commercial project. For anything about privacy, write to privacy@whencanistop.fyi; for anything else, to hello@whencanistop.fyi. If you write to either, your message and your address are kept in the operator's mailbox, at iCloud Mail (Apple), only to answer you, and deleted when they're no longer needed.
